research_rationale: Executive Order 6206-A (July 16, 1933) is a final approval, with amendments set out in Schedule A, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity, date and subject confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); the withdrawal of the termination condition leaves the approval without a four-month end. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.
savings_reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.
earlier_end_check: The order withdraws the earlier condition that terminated approval at the end of four months unless expressly renewed ("condition 12 of said order providing for the termination of approval at the end of four months unless expressly renewed"), so no four-month end applies to this final approval. Paragraph 5 of Schedule A begins "Until adoption of further provisions of this Code that may prove necessary", which is a term of the code that depends on later code provisions and not a limit on the approval, and paragraph 1 asks a code agency to report "prior to January 1, 1934", which is a deadline and not an end. Held later orders naming the Cotton Textile Code are: EO 6242-C, 6242-D and 6242-E (denials of company applications for exemption, each excepting the Administrator's stay of July 30, 1933 on the machine-hour provision as applied to tire yarns); EO 6407 and EO 6476 (denial of that exemption and termination of the stay, effective November 13 and December 11, 1933); EO 6424 and EO 6463 (extensions of the stay's termination date); EO 6420-A (approval of modifications "made a part of said code"); EO 6858 (September 26, 1934: creates the Textile Labor Relations Board and, in section 9, abolishes the Cotton Textile National Industrial Relations Board created by section XVII of the code as amended July 10, 1934); and EO 6876 (approval of an amendment). I read the operative paragraph of each. None cancels, suspends as a whole, supersedes or revokes the code approval: the stays reached one provision as applied to one product line and ended in 1933, EO 6858 concerns a board of the code's labor administration created by a July 1934 amendment, and EO 6420-A and EO 6876 are amendments, which are later events. No held record shows this code cancelled, suspended, superseded or revoked before June 14, 1935, and none shows a modification under section 10(b) that reached this order's command. June 16, 1935 is not an end, because section 1 of S.J. Res. 113 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date.
scope_check: One operative command: withdrawal of the termination condition and final approval of the code with the conditions accepted and the amendments proposed. Schedule A (attached to the order) sets out those amendments, including paragraph 1 (a function of the code's Planning and Fair Practice Agency to consider employee home ownership and report) and paragraphs 2 to 6 (hours, wage differentials, stretch-out, operation of the code). Each item is a term of the code approved by this command, with no force apart from the approval, so the single clause covers it. The conditions in paragraphs 1, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 13 of the July 9, 1933 order that the applicants accepted are not held in text; the only condition the held order describes as terminating approval is condition 12, which it withdraws.
independent_command_check: No appointment, delegation, direction to a government agency or other command independent of the code approval appears. The Planning and Fair Practice Agency named in Schedule A is an agency of the code itself, not of the government, and its report function exists only as a code term. The recital of the applicants' request and the Administrator's recommendation command nothing.
savings_check: Read S.J. Res. 113 section 2 and its proviso and NIRA section 5 in the packet excerpts. No held source continues this approval, a prosecution under it or any command of this order after June 14, 1935; accrued acts, liabilities and the section 5 exemption for completed action are recorded as transferred or accrued and not as continued operation.

research_rationale: Executive Order 6206-B (July 16, 1933) approves only certain provisions of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Thread Industry and does so "subject to the interpretations and conditions imposed by me on my approval of the corresponding provisions of said Cotton Textile Code and subject further to such revisions or modifications as I may find proper after a hearing has been held on said Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Thread Industry." The July 9, 1933 order that imposed those conditions is not held. EO 6206-A, signed the same day, describes that order as containing a condition 12 that terminated approval of the Cotton Textile Code "at the end of four months unless expressly renewed" and withdraws it for that code only. The held text does not show which conditions are incorporated or whether the four-month termination reaches the thread provisions; if it did, the approval would have ended about four months after July 17, 1933 unless renewed, long before the June 14, 1935 repeal. A search of the held texts for "Cotton Thread" finds only this order, so no record of the hearing, a final approval of the thread code or any renewal is held. The June 14, 1935 end therefore cannot be supported by held evidence.

research_rationale: Executive Order 6369 (October 31, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Dress Manufacturing Industry "subject to the following conditions" and contains stays that end on events the order leaves open: item 1 stays the western-area wage scale (except in the Chicago and Cleveland metropolitan areas) "until said determination", pending a further hearing, "further orders in this regard, and the final determination of the issues"; item 2 states how section 7 of article IV is read "during the period of such stay"; item 3 stays the application of the code to cotton house or wash dresses "pending the holding of such hearing on such notice as the Administrator in his discretion may fix, further orders in this regard and a final determination". The approval itself would end with the June 14, 1935 repeal, but each stay has its own end event, which may have occurred before June 14, 1935. No held record shows a hearing, order or determination on either issue: no held order text names the Dress Manufacturing Code other than this order, and the Administrator's orders are not in the held corpus. The repeal is therefore only an outer bound for the stays, and a first end of June 14, 1935 would assert without evidence that they survived to that date (owner ruling 2026-10-28: known within an interval is not the same as unknown whether).

research_rationale: Executive Order 6420-A (November 9, 1933) is a approval of modifications of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry, made part of the code under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Read in full from the held American Presidency Project transcription (page record checked; identity, date and subject confirmed against the census register and the WPA 1944 list); the order's own text states no limit on the approval. Its command depends entirely on the code approval, so its first end is the repeal of the code-approval and code-enforcement provisions of Title I by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, applying SHARED_ANALYSIS.md and its adjudication; Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization only.
savings_reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences, and the section 5 exemption from the antitrust laws for action complying with an approved code taken while Title I was in effect is likewise an accrued effect for completed action. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action under them, not codes, and states no time limit; the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the section 5 exemption for past action under codes, and whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect, not continued operation of this approval. Nothing in the held sources continues the approval after June 14, 1935.
earlier_end_check: The order states no period, "until" date, condition or provisional approval that limits the approval, and no stay or postponement to a fixed date. Held later orders naming the Cotton Textile Code are: EO 6242-C, 6242-D and 6242-E (denials of company applications for exemption, each excepting the Administrator's stay of July 30, 1933 on the machine-hour provision as applied to tire yarns); EO 6407 and EO 6476 (denial of that exemption and termination of the stay, effective November 13 and December 11, 1933); EO 6424 and EO 6463 (extensions of the stay's termination date); EO 6858 (September 26, 1934: creates the Textile Labor Relations Board and, in section 9, abolishes the Cotton Textile National Industrial Relations Board created by section XVII of the code as amended July 10, 1934); and EO 6876 (approval of an amendment). EO 6206-A, the final approval of the code, is an earlier order of July 16, 1933. I read the operative paragraph of each. None cancels, suspends as a whole, supersedes or revokes the code approval: the stays reached one provision as applied to one product line and ended in 1933, EO 6858 concerns a board of the code's labor administration created by a July 1934 amendment, and EO 6876 is an amendment, which is a later event. No held record shows this code cancelled, suspended, superseded or revoked before June 14, 1935, and none shows a modification under section 10(b) that reached this order's command. June 16, 1935 is not an end, because section 1 of S.J. Res. 113 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date.
scope_check: One operative command: approval of the modifications proposed by the Cotton Textile Industry Committee under sections 9 and 10 of the code, which the order makes "a part of said code". The held text does not reproduce the modifications; their content is not needed to date the end because each modification takes effect only as a term of the code approved under section 3, and the approval is what the repeal reached. The recital that the code was "approved July 9, 1933" repeats the date used in EO 6206-A and later orders for the original approval.
independent_command_check: No appointment, delegation, direction to a government agency, report direction or other command independent of the code approval appears. The "Approval recommended" and signature lines command nothing.
savings_check: Read S.J. Res. 113 section 2 and its proviso and NIRA section 5 in the packet excerpts. No held source continues this approval, a prosecution under it or any command of this order after June 14, 1935; accrued acts, liabilities and the section 5 exemption for completed action are recorded as transferred or accrued and not as continued operation.

research_rationale: Executive Order 6434 (November 17, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry "subject to the following conditions", and the only registered text is the American Presidency Project page captured from the Wayback Machine on 2023-09-04, which cannot be re-proven offline; the clause-drafts copy is not the registered text and is not quoted. The order is also a mixed order. Condition A treats a States' prison-labor compact as satisfying article VIII C of the code "if and so long as" the compact provides eight listed terms, and condition B stays section G of article IV for Kentucky and border counties of Illinois and Indiana "for such period as the Administrator shall determine, which period shall not exceed 4 months from and after the effective date of the aforesaid Code", requires the Administrator to hold hearings and to determine the classification of the area before the period ends. The effective date of the Cotton Garment Code, the Administrator's determination of the stay period and any compact adopted by the States are not held, so the stay's own-terms end and the compact condition cannot be dated.

research_rationale: Executive Order 6533 (December 23, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Electrotyping and Stereotyping Industry subject to two conditions, and condition 2 states: "That my approval of the Code as a separate Code is limited to a period of three (3) months from the effective date thereof, and the Administrator is hereby authorized, after such public notice and hearing as he may prescribe, to require the Electrotyping and Stereotyping Industry to operate under the Code of Fair Competition for the Graphic Arts Industries." That is an own-terms limit that, if not extended or replaced, ended the separate approval about three months after the code's effective date, long before June 14, 1935. The code's effective date is not stated in the order and no held text gives it; the only later held order naming the code, EO 6606-E (February 17, 1934), replaces condition 1 only and does not mention condition 2; and no held record shows whether the Administrator required the industry to operate under the Graphic Arts Code or extended the three months. The repeal date therefore cannot be supported as the first end, and the own-terms end cannot be computed.
